procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 09.07.2013 of the High Court of Judicature of Andhra Pradesh at Hyderabad in Criminal Appeal No. 340 of 2008 and Criminal R. C. No. 643 of 2008.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court exercised its appellate power under Section 386 Cr.P.C. and reversed the order of the Trial Court, substituting its own reasons. The High Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 340 of 2008 and Criminal R. C. No. 643 of 2008.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (likely the original accused) appealed to the Supreme Court, challenging the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and dismissed the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal passed by the Trial Court, especially when the view taken by the Trial Court is a possible or plausible one.

facts: The Trial Court acquitted the accused, in part by discarding the evidence of an injured witness and other eyewitnesses.
The High Court, exercising its appellate power, reversed the Trial Court's order of acquittal and convicted the accused.
The High Court found that the Trial Court's reasoning for discarding the eyewitness testimony was perverse.
law: The settled legal principle is that an appellate court should not interfere with a trial court's order of acquittal if the view taken by the trial court is a possible or plausible one.
If two reasonable views are possible—one leading to acquittal and the other to conviction—the appellate court must rule in favor of the accused.
However, an exception to this rule exists. An appellate court can and should interfere if the acquittal is perverse, manifestly illegal, or grossly unjust.
A 'perverse' finding is one that no reasonable person would have come to.
Under Section 386 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.), the High Court has full power to review the evidence and reverse an order of acquittal.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the reasoning of the Trial Court and agreed with the High Court's assessment.
It held that this was a case where the Trial Court's reasoning for discarding the evidence of the injured witness and other eyewitnesses was perverse.
Because the Trial Court's decision was found to be perverse, it did not qualify as a 'possible or plausible view.'
This perversity triggered the exception to the general rule, making it appropriate for the High Court to intervene.
The Supreme Court determined that the High Court correctly exercised its appellate powers under Section 386 Cr.P.C. to reverse the flawed acquittal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal, concluding that the High Court was justified in interfering with the Trial Court's order of acquittal. The Court reasoned that while an appellate court should not normally overturn a plausible acquittal, it is empowered to do so when the trial court's decision is perverse, as it was found to be in this case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal passed by the Trial Court, especially when the view taken by the Trial Court is a possible or plausible one.
appellant_arguments: The Trial Court's order of acquittal was based on a proper appreciation of evidence and should not have been interfered with by the High Court.
When two views are possible, the Appellate Court should not interfere with an order of acquittal.
The medical evidence presented by the prosecution did not support the ocular evidence from the eyewitnesses, which is why the Trial Court rightly disbelieved the prosecution's case.
The High Court wrongly placed the burden on the accused to prove certain facts, when the burden should have remained on the prosecution.
The doctor who testified was not shown the weapon to give an opinion on whether the injuries could have been caused by it.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was correct to reverse the acquittal.
The eyewitness accounts were reliable, and the Trial Court discarded their evidence for insufficient reasons.
The Trial Court wrongly dismissed the injured witnesses as 'interested witnesses' when they were family members accompanying the deceased and were in a position to prove the incident.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court, in exercising its appellate power, should not reverse a Trial Court's order of acquittal if the Trial Court's view is a possible or plausible one, even if the High Court's own view is also possible.
obiter: In exercise of Appellate power under Section 386 Cr.P.C. the High Court has full power to reverse an order of acquittal.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was justified in interfering with the Trial Court's acquittal because the Trial Court's reasoning was found to be perverse. Specifically, the Trial Court's decision to discard the credible evidence of an injured witness and other eyewitnesses was a conclusion that no reasonable person would have reached, thus meeting the exception to the general rule against appellate interference with acquittals.
legal_tests_applied: While an appellate court should not interfere with an acquittal if the Trial Court's view is a possible or plausible one, it has a duty to interfere if the acquittal is perverse, manifestly illegal, or grossly unjust.
An acquittal is considered perverse if no reasonable person would have come to that conclusion based on the evidence presented.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's reliance on the 'two possible views' doctrine failed because the Trial Court's view was not considered a reasonable or plausible one; it was deemed perverse.

The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court that the Trial Court's reasoning for discarding the evidence of the injured witness and other eyewitnesses was perverse, thereby justifying the reversal of the acquittal.
why_respondent_won: The High Court correctly exercised its appellate power by reversing the acquittal because the Trial Court's reasoning was found to be perverse.

The eyewitness accounts, particularly from the injured witness, were deemed reliable and sufficient to prove the prosecution's case, and the Trial Court's dismissal of this evidence was an error that warranted correction by the High Court.
